title: Strings: Encode and Decode a List of Strings
oneLiner: Pack a list of arbitrary strings into one string and unpack it again. Prefix each string with its length and a separator, so the content is never scanned for delimiters.
keyTakeaway: Any delimiter character can also appear inside the strings, so don't search for one. Write each string as length + '#' + string. To decode, read digits up to the next '#', which gives the length L, then take exactly the next L characters, whatever they contain. That is length-prefixed framing, the same idea network protocols use.
explanation:
Write Encode, which turns a list of strings into a single string, and Decode, which turns that string back into the original list. The strings may contain any characters, including commas, digits, # and nothing at all (empty strings). The grader checks that Decode(Encode(list)) gives the same list back.

Joining with a separator, such as a comma, breaks the moment a string contains a comma: ["a,b"] and ["a", "b"] encode the same. Escaping the separator works but is fiddly. The robust approach is to never look inside the strings at all: write each one's length in front of it.

Encode: for each s, append s.Length, then '#', then s. ["lint", "code"] becomes "4#lint4#code". Decode: start at i = 0. Find the next '#' from i, at j. The digits s[i..j) are the length L. The string is the L characters after the '#': s[j + 1 .. j + 1 + L). Append it and continue from i = j + 1 + L. A '#' inside a string is harmless, because by the time you reach it you are copying L characters, not searching.

Why the '#' is safe to search for: you only ever search for it right after the previous string ended, where the encoder wrote digits, so the first '#' you meet is always the one after the length. Both directions are O(n) in the total number of characters. HTTP's Content-Length header and most binary protocols frame messages exactly this way.

The visualization encodes ["a#b", "", "#x"] and decodes it again, piece by piece.

visualizationSteps.message: Encode ["a#b", "", "#x"] as length # string: "3#a#b0#2##x". The # inside the strings will not confuse the decoder.
At 0: digits up to the # at 1 say length 3. Copy the next 3 characters without looking at them: "a#b". Continue at 5.
At 5: digits up to the # at 6 say length 0. Copy the next 0 characters without looking at them: "". Continue at 7.
At 7: digits up to the # at 8 say length 2. Copy the next 2 characters without looking at them: "#x". Continue at 11.
Decoded the same three strings, including the empty one.

recognitionSignals: Serialize a list of arbitrary strings, or frame messages on a stream, where any delimiter could also be data.
"Design an encoding" with no restrictions on the characters in the input.
gotchas: Using a delimiter alone breaks on strings that contain it.
Empty strings must survive: "0#" encodes one, and [] must encode to something that decodes to [].
Lengths can have several digits (12#...), so read up to the '#', not one character.
confusableWith: Serialize and Deserialize a Binary Tree also round-trips a structure through a string; there the tokens are numbers, so a comma separator is safe.
Run-length encoding compresses repeated characters; this is about unambiguous framing, not size.

complexity.note: Here n is the total number of characters. Encoding writes each character once plus a short length prefix per string; decoding reads each character once. The encoded string and the decoded list are both O(n).

referenceSolutions.python:
def encode(strs):
    return "".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs)  # length first: no escaping needed


def decode(s):
    result = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(s):
        j = s.index("#", i)  # the first # after i always ends a length
        length = int(s[i:j])
        result.append(s[j + 1:j + 1 + length])  # copy, never search, the content
        i = j + 1 + length
    return result
